findings.evidence: Eligibility: "the home-office equipment stipend" and "However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt." Reimbursement Amounts (heading) over "The stipend pays up to 500 dollars per benefit year." Program Coordination: "schedules the reimbursement for the next pay cycle." Terminology Notes: "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review." Approval Timeline: "the equipment category matches the approved list" vs. Restrictions and Exceptions: "one device per category per employee."
findings.fix: Pick one term per concept (e.g., always "stipend payment" for the money, "equipment" for the physical item, "request" for the application) and use it throughout; if Terminology Notes is meant to define terms, have it actually state the equivalences.
findings.location: Throughout the document (Eligibility; Reimbursement Amounts heading vs. body; Program Coordination; Terminology Notes; Approval Timeline vs. Restrictions and Exceptions)
findings.violation: Several terms for what appears to be the same payment concept -- stipend, reimbursement, stipend request, stipend item -- and several terms for the physical thing covered -- equipment, device, item, category -- are used interchangeably with no defined-terms statement or stated equivalence anywhere, including in the one section titled Terminology Notes, which introduces "stipend item" without ever defining it or linking it to "stipend request" used elsewhere. A reader cannot tell whether these name the same thing or something narrower.

findings.evidence: "If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee."
findings.fix: Open with the governing rule, e.g. "The home-office equipment stipend is available once an employee meets all of the following:" and then list the three conditions.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with three separate conditional sentences before the fourth sentence finally states the governing rule, so the reader has to hold three unresolved conditions in mind and reach the end of the paragraph before the opening sentences make sense.

findings.evidence: Program Overview: "The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter." Overview (later section): "The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period."
findings.fix: Merge the two sections into one, state the publisher and cadence a single time, and delete the duplicate; if the process actually changed, state only the current rule and remove the superseded sentence.
findings.violation: Two separate, similarly named sections placed far apart both describe who publishes the reimbursement log and on what schedule, and they disagree -- people operations office publishing quarterly versus benefits team publishing after every open enrollment period -- with no cross-reference or signal anywhere in the document for which one governs. This is the shape of a document organized by appending content as it arrived rather than by what the reader needs to find once, in one place.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
